chapter_title: The Interpretation [of] the S[i]lence, the Fast, [the Peace], the Day, [and] the Rest; [what] they are.
chapter_note: Extremely fragmentary chapter preserving a five-fold cosmological teaching that maps ritual/devotional terms (Silence, Fast, Peace, Day, Rest) to cosmic archetypes. The substrate structure is a systematic five-fold enumeration mapping each term to a cosmic being or domain — classic correspondential pedagogy. Only fragments survive: Paragraph 3 preserves the clearest mapping (First Man / ship of living waters). The Pillar of Glory reference in P2 suggests another mapping. The chapter closes with a standard beatitude formula. Despite heavy damage, the oldest teaching layer is clearly dominant in what survives. Gardner's note that Mani provides 'cosmological archetypes for ritual practices' confirms the cosmos→cosmos mapping structure, though the editorial layer connecting these to community practice is largely lost or was minimal.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Very fragmentary but the visible content maps within the cosmic system. 'The gatherer' and 'the Pillar of Glory' are cosmic entities in the light-architecture. 'The body' and 'lusts of the world' in this context likely refer to the cosmic body and the forces of matter — part of the cosmological process description, not moral exhortation. 'Righteousness' here appears to describe a cosmic quality rather than an ethical injunction. This paragraph likely mapped one of the five terms (possibly 'the fast' or 'the silence') to the Pillar of Glory and the cosmic gathering process.

'The ship of living waters' is a cosmic vessel in the light-architecture (the moon). Both sides of the mapping stay within the system.
